catalog_quote: [Ramamurti 1931 sec. 8] The Sora: language has no doubt “stress” though it is not so sharp and striking as in English. ... It is, therefore, very difficult to determine the position of stress in every word. The following rules, tentatively deduced, may be helpful to the student. ... Stress is heard in— (1) The negative prefix ad as in 'aj-jumai ... (12) Generally the first syllable as in 'tuleb-on, ‘wood, forest’ ... Stress is not heard in— ... (2) The suffix -ən or -an added to form nouns or verbal nouns ... [Horo et al. 2023 p. 144] The original comments on the system of prominence in Sora comes from Gidugu (1931), who suggests that ... there is morphologically conditioned stress ... Donegan & Stampe (1983, 2004) ... claim that Sora rather is an example of a Quantity Sensitive trochaic stress pattern ... The latter claim has been proven to be inaccurate by instrumental and statistical…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated places (Ramamurti 1931 djvu the text layer = Part I sec. 8 pp. 6-7 + fn. 1; Horo et al. 2023 FASAL 12 the text layerp. 144 and 445-455 p. 166). (2) The classification 'conflict' rests on the only full early description (1931 manual, impressionistic, morphology-keyed rules with default initial stress) against the only dedicated prosodic work on the language (Horo et al. instrumental series 2015-2023: exceptionless second-syllable prominence in disyllables, cues split in 3-4 syllable words, Gidugu's morphological conditioning 'being subjected to rigorous testing'). Glottolog lists no phonology of Sora proper (Merlo 1920 is Sora, Italy) and no later grammar with a fuller stress treatment; Rao 1998 sec. 2.8 (held, Srikakulam) simply restates initial/morpheme-initial accent in Ramamurti's mould. (3) downloaded now: Horo 2017

sources.quote: Abstract: 'the acoustic analysis in this work confirms that Assam Sora has an iambic stress pattern where, the second syllable is more prominent then the first syllable in disyllables ... explained with the help of three phonetic cues, namely, vowel duration, fundamental frequency and vowel intensity.' p. 206: 'Regarding Orissa Sora, the word stress pattern is undescribed.' p. 216: 'by examining the three phonetic cues of word stress in Orissa Sora, it is confirmed that the second syllable in disyllables is more prominent than the first syllable ... this work proposes similar to Assam Sora, sy
sources.locator: Abstract (front matter); ch. 3 sec. 3.3-3.4 pp. 103-105ff; ch. 6 sec. 6.4 pp. 206-216 (Assam vs Orissa Sora); field sites sec. 1.x p. 39 (Raiguda, Gunupur block, Rayagada district, Odisha; Assam speakers 'originated from Ganjam district')
sources.note: The full instrumental study behind Horo et al. 2020/2023; ch. 6.4 extends second-syllable prominence to Odisha (Rayagada) Sora disyllables, i.e. a homeland lect, which weakens any 'Assam diaspora vs Ramamurti's Ganjam Sora' reconciliation of the conflict. downloaded now.

sources.quote: Abstract: 'Assam Sora words are minimally disyllabic ... The difference in vowel quality, vowel duration, f0 and vowel intensity between two syllables point towards the existence of iambic stress in Assam Sora disyllables.' (Singrijhan speakers only; the first instrumental statement, later generalised in Horo 2017/2020/2023.)

sources.note: First instrumental statement of iambic disyllabic stress, cited by the record's modern source; downloaded now for completeness.
